concepts: Cofactors and adjoint of a matrix
Change of base of logarithms
questions.question: Let $A=[a_{ij}]=\begin{pmatrix}\log_5 128 & \log_4 5\\ \log_5 8 & \log_4 25\end{pmatrix}$. If $A_{ij}$ is the cofactor of $a_{ij}$, $C_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{2}a_{ik}A_{jk}$, $1\le i,j\le 2$ and $C=[C_{ij}]$, then $8|C|$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $\sum_k a_{ik}A_{jk}$ is a row of $A$ times the cofactors of another row, so it equals $|A|\,\delta_{ij}$ and $C=|A|I$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A row times the cofactors of another row gives $|A|\delta_{ij}$, so $C=|A|I$ without computing any cofactor product.
solution: By the expansion theorem, $\sum_k a_{ik}A_{ik}=|A|$ and $\sum_k a_{ik}A_{jk}=0$ for $i\ne j$ (a determinant with two equal rows).

useful_results: For an $n\times n$ matrix, $\sum_k a_{ik}A_{jk}=|A|$ if $i=j$ and $0$ if $i\ne j$ (a row against another row's cofactors); in matrix form $A\,(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|I$.
So $C=A(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|I$, $|C|=|A|^n$ and $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$. Here $n=2$: $|C|=|A|^2=\left(\frac{11}{2}\right)^2$.
Log toolkit: $\log_ab\cdot\log_ba=1$ and $\log_{a^m}b^n=\frac nm\log_ab$. Here $\log_425=\log_25$ and $\log_5128\cdot\log_25=7$.

concepts: Geometric progression
questions.question: Let $a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots$ be a G.P. of increasing positive numbers. If $a_3a_5=729$ and $a_2+a_4=\frac{111}{4}$, then $24(a_1+a_2+a_3)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: In a G.P., $a_3a_5=a_4^2$, so the middle term $a_4$ comes out at once.
solution: Let the first term be $a$ and the common ratio $r$: $a_3a_5=ar^2\cdot ar^4=729$, so $(ar^3)^2=729$.
Divide: $\frac{ar^3}{ar}=\frac{27}{3/4}=36$, so $r^2=36$ and $r=6$ (the G.P. is increasing and positive).

alternate_solutions.idea: Work with the neighbours of the middle term: $a_3a_5=a_4^2$ gives $a_4$, then $a_2$, and the ratio follows from $a_4=a_2r^2$.
solution: $a_3a_5=a_4^2=729$ and all terms are positive, so $a_4=27$.

useful_results: In a G.P., $a_{m-k}\,a_{m+k}=a_m^2$. So $a_3a_5=a_4^2$ gives $a_4=27$ immediately (positive terms).
Terms two apart are linked by $r^2$: $a_4=a_2r^2$, which is often quicker than working with $a$ and $r$ together.
Increasing and positive means $r>1$ (and $a>0$): this selects $r=6$ over $r=-6$.

concepts: Arithmetic progression and its sum
questions.question: Consider an A.P. of positive integers, whose sum of the first three terms is $54$ and the sum of the first twenty terms lies between $1600$ and $1800$. Then its $11^{th}$ term is :
questions.key_idea: Write the first three terms as $18-d,\ 18,\ 18+d$, so only the common difference $d$ is unknown and $S_{20}$ confines it to one integer.
solution: Let the first three terms be $a-d,\ a,\ a+d$. Their sum is $3a=54$, so $a=18$.
The terms are $18-d,\ 18,\ 18+d$; the first term is $18-d$ and the common difference is $d$.
The terms are integers, so $d$ is an integer: $d=8$. The first term is $18-8=10$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Express $T_{11}=18+9d$, so only two options give an integer $d$; test those against $S_{20}$.
solution: The middle of the first three terms is $T_2=18$ (sum $54$ divided by $3$).
Check the options: $90\Rightarrow d=8$; $108\Rightarrow d=10$; $122\Rightarrow d=\frac{104}{9}$ and $84\Rightarrow d=\frac{22}{3}$ are not integers.

useful_results: Three terms of an A.P. with known sum: take $a-d,\ a,\ a+d$; the middle term is (sum)/3.

$S_{20}=20\times(\text{mean of the 20 terms})=20\left(T_2+8.5d\right)$ here, which grows by $170$ for each unit increase in $d$; a window of width $200$ therefore holds at most two integer values of $d$.
If the options are numbers, test them first: $T_{11}=T_2+9d=18+9d$ must be an integer value of the form $18+9d$ with integer $d$.

concepts: Adjoint of a 2×2 matrix and its powers
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=I+\operatorname{adj}(A)+(\operatorname{adj}A)^2+\dots+(\operatorname{adj}A)^{10}$. Then, the sum of all the elements of the matrix $B$ is :
questions.key_idea: $\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has powers $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $B$ is a sum of such matrices.
solution: For a $2\times2$ matrix, $\operatorname{adj}A$ swaps the diagonal and negates the off-diagonal: $\operatorname{adj}(A)=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
Each diagonal entry is $1+1+\dots+1=11$. The upper right entry is $-2(0+1+2+\dots+10)=-110$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\operatorname{adj}A=I-2E$ with $E^2=O$, so every power collapses by the binomial theorem: $(I-2E)^k=I-2kE$.
solution: Since $I$ and $E$ commute and $E^2=O$, $(I-2E)^k=I-2kE$ for every $k\ge0$.
$B=\begin{pmatrix}11&-110\\0&11\end{pmatrix}$ and the sum of all elements is $11+11-110=-88$.

useful_results: For $N=I+tE$ with $E^2=O$ (nilpotent), $N^k=I+ktE$. Here $E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $t=-2$.
$\operatorname{adj}\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}s&-q\\-r&p\end{pmatrix}$; when $|A|=1$, $\operatorname{adj}A=A^{-1}$ (here $A^{-1}$ is $A$ with $2\to-2$).

concepts: Relation between roots and coefficients of a quadratic
questions.question: If $2$ and $6$ are the roots of the equation $ax^2+bx+1=0$, then the quadratic equation, whose roots are $\frac{1}{2a+b}$ and $\frac{1}{6a+b}$, is :
questions.key_idea: Sum and product of the roots $2,6$ give $a$ and $b$; the new roots then come from $2a+b$ and $6a+b$.
solution: For the roots $2$ and $6$: sum $=8=-\frac ba$ and product $=12=\frac1a$.
$2a+b=\frac{2}{12}-\frac23=-\frac12$, so the first new root is $\frac{1}{2a+b}=-2$.
$6a+b=\frac{6}{12}-\frac23=-\frac16$, so the second new root is $\frac{1}{6a+b}=-6$.
Sum of new roots $=-8$ and product of new roots $=12$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF finds the sum of the new roots (-8) and then writes x^2+8x+12=0 without computing their product; the product of the new roots (-2)(-6)=12 is added as a step. The answer is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $2$ is a root, $4a+2b+1=0$ gives $2a+b=-\frac12$ directly; likewise $6a+b=-\frac16$. No need to find $a$ and $b$.
solution: The new roots are $-2$ and $-6$: sum $-8$, product $12$.

useful_results: If $r$ is a root of $ax^2+bx+c=0$ then $ar^2+br+c=0$, so $ar+b=-\frac cr$ ($r\ne0$). Hence $\frac{1}{ar+b}=-\frac rc$.
So the numbers $\frac1{ar_i+b}$ built from the roots $r_i$ are just $-\frac{r_i}{c}$ -- here $-2$ and $-6$ ($c=1$).
Quadratic with roots $p,q$: $x^2-(p+q)x+pq=0$. Always compute both the sum and the product.

concepts: Matrix multiplication and powers of a matrix
questions.question: Let $A=[a_{ij}]$ be a matrix of order $3\times3$, with $a_{ij}=(\sqrt2)^{i+j}$. If the sum of all the elements in the third row of $A^2$ is $\alpha+\beta\sqrt2$, $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Z$, then $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Every entry carries $(\sqrt2)^{i+j}$, so $A$ is a scalar multiple of a simple matrix and only the third row of $A^2$ is needed.
solution: Third row of the square, entry 1: $2\cdot1+2\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2+4\cdot2=2+4+8=14$.
Sum of the third row of $A^2=4\left(14+14\sqrt2+28\right)=4\left(42+14\sqrt2\right)=168+56\sqrt2$.
useful_results: If $a_{ij}=u_iu_j$ then $A=uu^{T}$ has rank one and $A^2=(u^Tu)\,A$, so $A^n=(u^Tu)^{n-1}A$.
For $a_{ij}=x^{i+j}$, $u=(x,x^2,\dots,x^n)^T$; the entries of any power are again of the form $c\,x^{i+j}$.
The sum of the elements in a row of $M$ is the corresponding entry of $M\mathbf 1$ (multiply by the all-ones column).

concepts: Sum of a series by telescoping (method of differences)
questions.question: If the sum of the first $20$ terms of the series $\frac{4\cdot1}{4+3\cdot1^2+1^4}+\frac{4\cdot2}{4+3\cdot2^2+2^4}+\frac{4\cdot3}{4+3\cdot3^2+3^4}+\frac{4\cdot4}{4+3\cdot4^2+4^4}+\dots$ is $\frac mn$, where $m$ and $n$ are coprime, then $m+n$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $r^4+3r^2+4=(r^2+2)^2-r^2=(r^2+r+2)(r^2-r+2)$ splits the term into a difference of two consecutive values of $\frac1{r^2-r+2}$.
solution: Since $(r+1)^2-(r+1)+2=r^2+r+2$, the second part of $T_r$ cancels the first part of $T_{r+1}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Guess the closed form of $S_n$ from the first partial sums and confirm it by induction. (A lighter variant, not a radically new method.)
solution: So the formula holds for all $n$, and $S_{20}=\frac{20\cdot21}{422}=\frac{210}{211}$.

useful_results: Sophie Germain pattern: $r^4+3r^2+4=(r^2+2)^2-r^2$, and in general $x^4+4y^4=(x^2+2y^2+2xy)(x^2+2y^2-2xy)$.

Telescoping rule: if $g(r+1)-g(r)=k\cdot(\text{numerator})$ then $\frac{\text{numerator}}{g(r)g(r+1)}=\frac1k\left[\frac1{g(r)}-\frac1{g(r+1)}\right]$. Here $g(r)=r^2-r+2$, $g(r+1)=r^2+r+2$, $g(r+1)-g(r)=2r$.
For this series $S_n=\frac{n(n+1)}{n^2+n+2}$ (e.g. $S_1=\frac12$, $S_2=\frac34$); $n=20$ gives $\frac{420}{422}$.

concepts: Inverse, similarity and characteristic equation of a matrix
questions.question: Let $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\1&5\end{pmatrix}$ and $A$ be a $2\times2$ matrix such that $AB^{-1}=A^{-1}$. If $BCB^{-1}=A$ and $C^4+\alpha C^2+\beta I=O$, then $2\beta-\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $BCB^{-1}=A$ makes $C$ similar to $A$, so $C^2=B^{-1}A^2B=B$ and $C^4=B^2$; the equation becomes $B^2+\alpha B+\beta I=O$.
solution: $AB^{-1}=A^{-1}$; multiplying on the right by $B$ gives $A=A^{-1}B$, and then on the left by $A$ gives $A^2=B$.
So $\alpha=-6$ and $\beta=2$ (the other two entries, $6+\alpha=0$ and $28+5\alpha+\beta=0$, hold too).

alternate_solutions.idea: After reducing to $B^2+\alpha B+\beta I=O$, recognise it as the Cayley--Hamilton equation of $B$: $\alpha=-\operatorname{tr}B$, $\beta=\det B$.
solution: As before, $C^4+\alpha C^2+\beta I=O$ reduces to $B^2+\alpha B+\beta I=O$.
$B$ is a $2\times2$ matrix, not a scalar matrix, so no linear relation $B=kI$ holds; a monic quadratic relation satisfied by $B$ is therefore unique.
By Cayley--Hamilton, $B^2-(\operatorname{tr}B)B+(\det B)I=O$ is such a relation.

useful_results: $AB^{-1}=A^{-1}\Rightarrow A^2=B$. Similar matrices: $(P^{-1}XP)^n=P^{-1}X^nP$.
Cayley--Hamilton for $2\times2$: $B^2-(\operatorname{tr}B)B+(\det B)I=O$. If $B$ is not a scalar matrix, this is the only monic quadratic relation $B$ satisfies.
For $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\1&5\end{pmatrix}$: $\operatorname{tr}B=6$, $\det B=2$, so $B^2-6B+2I=O$ (matches $\alpha=-6$, $\beta=2$).

concepts: Sum of a series by telescoping (method of differences)
questions.question: The sum of the series $\frac{1}{1-3\cdot1^2+1^4}+\frac{2}{1-3\cdot2^2+2^4}+\frac{3}{1-3\cdot3^2+3^4}+\dots$ upto $10$-terms is :
questions.key_idea: $r^4-3r^2+1=(r^2-1)^2-r^2$ factors, and $r$ is half the difference of the two factors, so the sum telescopes.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compute the first partial sums, guess $S_n=-\frac{n(n+1)}{2(n^2+n-1)}$ and verify it. (A lighter variant, not a radically new method.)
solution: The values $-1,-\frac35,-\frac6{11}$ fit $S_n=-\frac{n(n+1)}{2(n^2+n-1)}$: denominators $2\cdot1,\ 2\cdot5,\ 2\cdot11$ and numerators $2,6,12$ (over $2$).

useful_results: Same pattern as the previous question: $r^4-3r^2+1=(r^2-r-1)(r^2+r-1)$, with $g(r)=r^2-r-1$ and $g(r+1)=r^2+r-1$.
For this series $S_n=-\frac12\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{n^2+n-1}$ (e.g. $S_1=-1$, $S_2=-\frac35$, $S_{10}=-\frac{55}{109}$).
Recognition cue: quartic denominators of the form $x^4+px^2+q$ with a numerator proportional to $x$ are tried as a difference of squares.

concepts: Geometric progression
Relation between roots and coefficients of a quadratic
questions.question: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of the equation $px^2+qx-r=0$, where $p\ne0$. If $p$, $q$ and $r$ are the consecutive terms of a non constant G.P. and $\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=\frac34$, then the value of $(\alpha-\beta)^2$ is :
questions.key_idea: $\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}=\frac{-q/p}{-r/p}=\frac qr$ fixes the G.P. ratio, then $(\alpha-\beta)^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Divide by $p$: with ratio $R$ the equation is $x^2+Rx-R^2=0$, so $\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=\frac1R$ immediately.
solution: Let the ratio of the G.P. be $R$, so $q=pR$ and $r=pR^2$. Dividing by $p$: $x^2+Rx-R^2=0$.

useful_results: For the roots of $px^2+qx+s=0$: $\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=-\frac qs$. With $s=-r$ this is $\frac qr$.
If $p,q,r$ are in G.P. with ratio $R$, divide by $p$: the equation becomes $x^2+Rx-R^2=0$, so $\alpha+\beta=-R$, $\alpha\beta=-R^2$ and $\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=\frac1R$.
Then $(\alpha-\beta)^2=R^2+4R^2=5R^2$ (here $R=\frac43$ gives $\frac{80}{9}$).

concepts: Properties of determinants
questions.question:
If $\alpha
e a,\  eta
e b,\ \gamma
e c$ and $ egin{vmatrix}\alpha&b&c\a& eta&c\a&b&\gamma\end{vmatrix}=0$, then $ rac{a}{\alpha-a}+ rac{b}{ eta-b}+ rac{\gamma}{\gamma-c}$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $R_1\to R_1-R_2$ and $R_2\to R_2-R_3$ create zeros, and dividing the expansion by $(\alpha-a)(\beta-b)(\gamma-c)$ gives the required sum.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the matrix as $D+\mathbf 1\,(a,b,c)$ with $D$ diagonal; the matrix determinant lemma gives $1+\sum\frac{a}{\alpha-a}=0$ at once.
solution: Subtract the diagonal $D=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha-a,\ \beta-b,\ \gamma-c)$: what remains has every row equal to $(a,b,c)$.
So the matrix is $D+\mathbf 1\,w^T$ with $\mathbf 1=(1,1,1)^T$ and $w=(a,b,c)^T$.
The determinant is $0$ and $\det D\ne0$, so $\frac{a}{\alpha-a}+\frac{b}{\beta-b}+\frac{c}{\gamma-c}=-1$.
Now $\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-c}=1+\frac{c}{\gamma-c}$, so the required sum is $-1+1=0$.

useful_results: Matrix determinant lemma: $\det(D+u\,w^T)=\det D\,\left(1+w^TD^{-1}u\right)$ for invertible $D$. Here $D=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha-a,\beta-b,\gamma-c)$, $u=(1,1,1)^T$, $w=(a,b,c)^T$.
Consequently $\begin{vmatrix}\alpha&b&c\\a&\beta&c\\a&b&\gamma\end{vmatrix}=0\iff\frac{a}{\alpha-a}+\frac{b}{\beta-b}+\frac{c}{\gamma-c}=-1$.
Because $\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-c}=1+\frac{c}{\gamma-c}$, the question's sum is $-1+1=0$.

concepts: Arithmetic progression (sums of odd and even placed terms)
questions.question: The number of terms of an A.P. is even; the sum of all the odd terms is $24$, the sum of all the even terms is $30$ and the last term exceeds the first by $\frac{21}{2}$. Then the number of terms which are integers in the A.P. is :
questions.key_idea: Subtracting the two sums pairs the terms and gives $nd=6$; the last-minus-first condition gives $(2n-1)d=\frac{21}2$.
solution: Let the number of terms be $2n$, with first term $a$ and common difference $d$: $T_1+T_3+\dots+T_{2n-1}=24$ and $T_2+T_4+\dots+T_{2n}=30$.
Then $n=\frac6d=4$, so the A.P. has $8$ terms.
The odd-placed terms are $n$ terms with common difference $2d$: $n\left(a+(n-1)d\right)=24$, i.e. $4\left(a+\frac92\right)=24$, so $a=\frac32$.
The integer terms are $3,\ 6,\ 9,\ 12$: there are $4$ of them.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the last-minus-first condition as (a+(2n+1)d)-a = 21/2; the last term is T_{2n}=a+(2n-1)d, so it should be (2n-1)d (the PDF's next line 2nd-d=21/2 already uses this). The PDF also states 'integral terms = 4' without showing the terms; a=3/2 and the list of terms were added. Answer (B) 4 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Divide the two conditions $(2n-1)d=\frac{21}2$ and $nd=6$ so that $d$ cancels and $n$ appears alone.
solution: $8n-4=7n$, so $n=4$ and the A.P. has $8$ terms; then $d=\frac64=\frac32$.
$T_k=\frac32k$ for $k=1,\dots,8$ is an integer exactly when $k$ is even: $k=2,4,6,8$, i.e. $4$ terms.

useful_results: For an A.P. with $2n$ terms: $S_{\text{even}}-S_{\text{odd}}=nd$ and $T_{\text{last}}-T_{\text{first}}=(2n-1)d$.
Dividing them: $\frac{(2n-1)d}{nd}=\frac{T_{\text{last}}-T_{\text{first}}}{S_{\text{even}}-S_{\text{odd}}}=\rho$ gives $n=\frac{1}{2-\rho}$ ($\rho=\frac74$ here, $n=4$).
With $a=d=\frac32$ the $k^{th}$ term is $\frac32k$: it is an integer exactly for even $k$. Always list the terms (or write $T_k$ in closed form) before counting integer terms.

concepts: Nature of roots of a quadratic equation (discriminant)
Sum of squares of natural numbers
questions.question: If the set of all $a\in\mathbb R$, for which the equation $2x^2+(a-5)x+15=3a$ has no real roots, is the interval $(\alpha,\beta)$ and $X=\{x\in\mathbb Z:\alpha<x<\beta\}$, then $\sum_{x\in X}x^2$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: No real roots means discriminant $<0$, which gives $(\alpha,\beta)=(-19,5)$; the integers $-18,\dots,4$ then need only $\sum k^2$.
solution: Write the equation as $2x^2+(a-5)x+(15-3a)=0$. It has no real roots when the discriminant is negative.
$\sum_{x\in X}x^2=(1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2)+(1^2+2^2+\dots+18^2)$ (the term $0$ adds nothing and each negative integer pairs with a positive one up to $18$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's second line reads 'a^2+14a+25-120<0' (it drops the -10a and the 24a of the expansion separately); the correct expansion is a^2-10a+25-120+24a = a^2+14a-95. The next line and the answer (C) 2139 are right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Separate the parameter: $a=-\frac{2x^2-5x+15}{x-3}$, and find its range with AM--GM; the missing values of $a$ are the ones giving no real root.
solution: Rewrite as $2x^2-5x+15+a(x-3)=0$. At $x=3$ the left side is $18\ne0$, so $x\ne3$ for any root and $a=-\frac{2x^2-5x+15}{x-3}$.
A real root exists exactly when $a\le-19$ or $a\ge5$, so there is no real root for $a\in(-19,5)$.

useful_results: If a parameter enters an equation linearly, solve for it: $a=g(x)$. The equation has a real root exactly when $a$ lies in the range of $g$.
AM--GM with signs: for $t>0$, $t+\frac kt\ge2\sqrt k$; for $t<0$, $t+\frac kt\le-2\sqrt k$ ($k>0$).
$\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$: $n=4$ gives $30$ and $n=18$ gives $2109$. Symmetric integer sets $\{-m,\dots,n\}$ give $\sum_1^m+\sum_1^n$.

concepts: Roots of a quadratic equation: power sums and recurrence
questions.question: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $x^2+\sqrt3x-16=0$, and $\gamma$ and $\delta$ be the roots of $x^2+3x-1=0$. If $P_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$ and $Q_n=\gamma^n+\delta^n$, then $\frac{P_{25}+\sqrt3P_{24}}{2P_{23}}+\frac{Q_{25}-Q_{23}}{Q_{24}}$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Each root satisfies its own equation, so multiplying by $x^{n-2}$ and adding the two roots gives a three-term recurrence for $P_n$ and $Q_n$.
solution: $\alpha^2+\sqrt3\alpha-16=0$; multiply by $\alpha^{n-2}$ and add the same for $\beta$: $P_n+\sqrt3P_{n-1}-16P_{n-2}=0$.
useful_results: For $x^2+bx+c=0$: $P_n+bP_{n-1}+cP_{n-2}=0$ ($n\ge2$), where $P_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$.
So $\frac{P_{n+2}+bP_{n+1}}{P_n}=-c$ whenever $P_n\ne0$. Here $-c=16$ and the ratio is $\frac{16P_{23}}{2P_{23}}=8$.

Check on $x^2+3x-1$: $Q_0=2,\ Q_1=-3,\ Q_2=11$ and $Q_2-Q_0=9=-3Q_1$, as the recurrence $Q_{n+2}-Q_n=-3Q_{n+1}$ predicts. The denominators are non-zero: $P_{23}<0$ (the negative root has the larger modulus) and $Q_{24}>0$.

concepts: Properties of determinants
Relation between roots and coefficients of a quadratic
questions.question: If $\begin{vmatrix}x+1&x&x\\x&x+\lambda&x\\x&x&x+\lambda^2\end{vmatrix}=\frac98(103x+81)$, then $\lambda,\frac\lambda3$ are the roots of the equation :
questions.key_idea: The identity holds for every $x$, so $x=0$ turns the determinant into a diagonal one and fixes $\lambda$.
solution: Sum of the roots $=\frac92+\frac32=6$ and product $=\frac92\cdot\frac32=\frac{27}{4}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda,\lambda^2)+x\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T$, so its determinant is linear in $x$: $\lambda^3+x(\lambda^3+\lambda^2+\lambda)$; compare both coefficients.
solution: Check the coefficient of $x$: $\lambda^3+\lambda^2+\lambda=\frac{729}{8}+\frac{81}4+\frac92=\frac{927}{8}=\frac98\cdot103$. It matches.
The roots are $\frac92$ and $\frac32$ (sum $6$, product $\frac{27}{4}$), giving $4x^2-24x+27=0$.

useful_results: Determinant of $D+x\,\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n)$: $\det D\left(1+x\sum\frac1{d_i}\right)$, which is always linear in $x$.
Here $d=(1,\lambda,\lambda^2)$: the determinant is $\lambda^3+x(\lambda^3+\lambda^2+\lambda)$.
Identity in $x$: compare coefficients or substitute a convenient value ($x=0$) instead of expanding fully.

concepts: Adjoint and determinant of a matrix (properties)
questions.question: Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and $A$ be a matrix of order $3\times3$ such that $\det(A)=-4$ and $A+I=\begin{pmatrix}1&a&1\\2&1&0\\a&1&2\end{pmatrix}$, where $I$ is the identity matrix of order $3\times3$. If $\det\left((a+1)\operatorname{adj}\left((a-1)A\right)\right)=2^m3^n$, $m,n\in\{0,1,2,\dots,20\}$, then $m+n$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: First $\det A=-4$ fixes $a=3$; then $(a+1)=4$ and $(a-1)A=2A$, and the adjoint rules $\operatorname{adj}(kA)=k^2\operatorname{adj}A$, $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^2$ finish.
solution: With $a=3$: $a+1=4$ and $a-1=2$, so the matrix is $4\operatorname{adj}(2A)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF treats (a-1)A as 3A (and writes |4 adj 3A| = 4^3 |3A|^2 = 64 (3^3)^2 |A|^2 = 2^6 3^6 16), giving m=10, n=6. With a=3, (a-1)A=2A, so the value is 64*(2^3)^2*16 = 2^16, i.e. m=16, n=0. Both give m+n=16, so answer (C) is unchanged.

solution: As before $a=3$, so the matrix is $4\operatorname{adj}(2A)$.

useful_results: For an $n\times n$ matrix: $\operatorname{adj}(kA)=k^{n-1}\operatorname{adj}A$, $|kA|=k^n|A|$, $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$ and $\operatorname{adj}A=|A|A^{-1}$.
Read the scalar off carefully: $(a-1)A$ with $a=3$ is $2A$, not $3A$.
For $n=3$: $\left|c\operatorname{adj}M\right|=c^3|M|^2$. With $c=4$, $M=2A$: $64\cdot(8\cdot(-4))^2=2^{16}$. Exponents must be matched with prime bases: $2^{16}=2^m3^n$ forces $n=0$.

concepts: Arithmetic progression (sums of odd and even placed terms)
questions.question: Suppose that the number of terms in an A.P. is $2k$, $k\in\mathbb N$. If the sum of all odd terms of the A.P. is $40$, the sum of all even terms is $55$ and the last term of the A.P. exceeds the first term by $27$, then $k$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Odd-placed and even-placed terms are two A.P.s of $k$ terms with common difference $2d$; subtracting the sums gives $kd$.
solution: Let the A.P. be $a,\ a+d,\ a+2d,\dots$ with $2k$ terms.
Even terms $T_2+T_4+\dots$ ($k$ terms): $(a+d)+(a+3d)+(a+5d)+\dots=55$, so $\frac k2\left\{2(a+d)+(k-1)2d\right\}=55$, i.e. $k(a+kd)=55$. (2)

alternate_solutions.idea: Divide the two relations $(2k-1)d=27$ and $kd=15$ so that $d$ cancels and $k$ is found directly.
solution: Pair the terms: $(T_2-T_1)+(T_4-T_3)+\dots+(T_{2k}-T_{2k-1})=55-40$, and each bracket is $d$, so $kd=15$.
Check: $k\left(a+(k-1)d\right)=40$ gives $a=-4$; the odd terms $-4,2,8,14,20$ sum to $40$ and the even terms $-1,5,11,17,23$ sum to $55$.

useful_results: For a $2k$-term A.P.: $S_{\text{even}}-S_{\text{odd}}=kd$ and $T_{\text{last}}-T_{\text{first}}=(2k-1)d$.
So $\frac{2k-1}{k}=\frac{T_{\text{last}}-T_{\text{first}}}{S_{\text{even}}-S_{\text{odd}}}=\frac{27}{15}$, i.e. $k=\frac1{2-27/15}=5$.
The same structure appears in the earlier even-term A.P. question; only the numbers change. Check by building the A.P.: $a=-4,\ d=3,\ k=5$ gives odd sum $40$ and even sum $55$.

concepts: Sum of a series by the method of differences
questions.question: The sum $1+3+11+25+45+71+\dots$ upto $20$ terms, is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The differences $2,8,14,20,\dots$ form an A.P., so $T_n$ is a quadratic in $n$.
solution: Write it again shifted by one place: $S_n=\ \ \ \ 1+3+11+25+45+\dots+T_{n-1}+T_n$.
Subtract: $0=1+2+8+14+20+\dots-T_n$ (the terms $2,8,14,20,\dots$ are the successive differences).
So $T_n=1+\left[2+8+14+\dots\ (n-1\text{ terms})\right]$, an A.P. with first term $2$ and common difference $6$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the difference table $1;\ 2;\ 6$ and the hockey-stick identity: $S_{N}=\binom N1\cdot1+\binom N2\cdot2+\binom N3\cdot6$.
solution: The terms are $1,3,11,25,45,71$; first differences $2,8,14,20,26$; second differences all $6$.
So the leading entries of the difference table are $\Delta^0T_1=1$, $\Delta^1T_1=2$, $\Delta^2T_1=6$ and all higher differences vanish.
Summing and using $\sum_{n=1}^{N}\binom{n-1}{j}=\binom{N}{j+1}$: $S_N=\binom N1+2\binom N2+6\binom N3$.

useful_results: If the first differences form an A.P. (second differences constant), the sequence is a quadratic polynomial in $n$.
Newton's form: $T_n=\sum_j\binom{n-1}{j}\Delta^jT_1$, and by the hockey-stick identity $\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_n=\sum_j\binom{N}{j+1}\Delta^jT_1$. Here $\Delta^0=1$, $\Delta^1=2$, $\Delta^2=6$.
Check on $N=3$: $3\cdot1+3\cdot2+1\cdot6=15=1+3+11$.

concepts: Properties of determinants (similar matrices)
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&2\\6&2&11\\3&3&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\5&0&2\\7&1&5\end{pmatrix}$. The sum of the prime factors of $|P^{-1}AP-2I|$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $P^{-1}AP-2I=P^{-1}(A-2I)P$, so the determinant equals $|A-2I|$ and $P$ never has to be inverted.
solution: $69=3\times23$, so the prime factors are $3$ and $23$ and their sum is $26$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Via the characteristic polynomial: $|A-2I|=-p_A(2)$ where $p_A(t)=t^3-(\operatorname{tr}A)t^2+(\text{sum of principal }2\times2\text{ minors})t-|A|$. (Valid but not shorter than the direct determinant.)

useful_results: Similar matrices have equal determinants: $|P^{-1}XP|=|X|$. In particular $P^{-1}AP-\lambda I=P^{-1}(A-\lambda I)P$, so $|P^{-1}AP-\lambda I|=|A-\lambda I|$ for every $\lambda$ (same characteristic polynomial).
Never compute $P^{-1}$ or $P$-products for such a question; the matrix $P$ only needs to be invertible.
Prime factors: $69=3\cdot23$; the 'sum of prime factors' counts each distinct prime once ($3+23=26$).

concepts: Properties of determinants (adjoint, transpose)
questions.question: Let $\alpha\in(0,\infty)$ and $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&\alpha\\1&0&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}$. If $\det\left(\operatorname{adj}(2A-A^T)\cdot\operatorname{adj}(A-2A^T)\right)=2^8$, then $(\det(A))^2$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Since $(A-2A^T)^T=-(2A-A^T)$ and the order is odd, $|A-2A^T|=-|2A-A^T|$, so the product of the two determinants is $-|2A-A^T|^2$.
solution: Let $M=2A-A^T$ and $N=A-2A^T$. For a $3\times3$ matrix $|\operatorname{adj}X|=|X|^2$, so $|\operatorname{adj}M\cdot\operatorname{adj}N|=|M|^2|N|^2=2^8$ and $|M||N|=\pm16$.
Expand $|N|$ along the second column; only the $(3,2)$ entry $-1$ is non-zero, with cofactor sign $(-1)^{3+2}=-1$ and minor $\begin{vmatrix}-1&\alpha\\-3&-1\end{vmatrix}=1+3\alpha$.
useful_results: For an $n\times n$ matrix: $|\operatorname{adj}X|=|X|^{n-1}$, $|X^T|=|X|$, $|kX|=k^n|X|$; for odd $n$, $|-X|=-|X|$.
If $N^T=-M$ with $n$ odd then $|N|=-|M|$, so $|M||N|=-|M|^2$ is never positive.
For this $A$: $|A|=\alpha-5$, $|2A-A^T|=-(3\alpha+1)$ and $|A-2A^T|=3\alpha+1$ (check at $\alpha=1$: $-4$, $-4$ and $4$ with $|A|=-4$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's notation is confusing (it names Q=2A^T-A and uses P for A-2A^T) and it asserts |A-2A^T|=4 although |M|^2=16 only gives |N|=±4; the choice of the positive sign needs alpha>0 (1+3 alpha=-4 would make alpha negative). This argument is added; the answer (B) 16 is unchanged.
